Why do cats love boxes so much?
You buy your cat a fancy new bed and it ignores it completely.
Then it climbs straight into the cardboard box the bed came in.
So what is it about a plain old box
that a cat just can't resist?
A parcel turns up at your door on a quiet afternoon.
You carry it inside and set it down on the floor.
You open it up and lift out whatever you ordered.
Maybe it's a lamp or a pair of shoes
or a lovely new cat tree. And before you've even folded the flaps
down there's a cat sitting inside the box.
It doesn't matter how big the box is.
It doesn't matter if the cat barely fits.
A big chunky cat will happily cram itself
into a tiny shoe box with its sides spilling over the edges.
Then it just sits there looking extremely pleased with itself.
Meanwhile the expensive thing that came
in the box lies forgotten on the floor.
People joke about this constantly. You can spend a small fortune on toys
and the cat would still rather have the packaging.
But there are real reasons hiding behind it.
Some of them go back thousands of years
and some are about how a cat feels on the inside.
Let's start with the oldest one.
Your house cat comes from a small wild cat
that lived in deserts and dry grasslands.
That wild cat was a hunter.
But it was also small enough to end up as somebody else's lunch.
Foxes and jackals and birds of prey
and bigger cats would all have been glad to eat it.
So a small wild cat needed two things at the same time.
It needed a way to hunt
and it needed a way to stay out of sight.
The answer to both turned out to be a good hiding spot.
Think of a gap between two rocks
or a hollow under a thorny bush.
Or maybe an old burrow dug into the ground by some other animal.
Somewhere small and dark with walls on every side.
Tucked in there the cat could rest without anything creeping up behind it.
And it could watch the world outside without being seen.
Cats are what scientists call ambush hunters.
They don't chase prey for miles the way wolves do.
Instead they wait patiently and quietly.
They hide somewhere still and they barely move a whisker.
Then when a mouse wanders close enough they explode out
in one fast pounce. For an ambush hunter a good hiding
spot is the most important tool there is.
Now look at a cardboard box the way your cat does.
It has walls on every side.
It has one opening to peek out of.
It's just big enough for one cat.
Honestly it's pretty much the perfect hunting hide.
Your cat sits in there with only its eyes and ears poking out.
It feels safe and it feels ready for action.
Anything that wanders past is about to get ambushed.
And quite often that something turns out to be your ankle.
The second big reason is stress.
Cats are animals that like things to stay the same.
They like the same food
and the same routine and the same quiet corners.
When something changes they can get anxious pretty quickly.
A new house or a new pet
or a loud party can all rattle a cat.
And when a cat feels stressed its first instinct is usually to hide.
Scientists have actually put this to the test.
In 2014 a team at Utrecht University in the Netherlands studied cats
that had just arrived at an animal shelter.
A shelter is a really stressful place for a cat.
Everything is new and noisy and smells of strangers.
Some of the new arrivals were given a box to hide in.
The others didn't get one.
The cats with boxes settled in much faster.
Within a few days they were calmer
and less stressed than the cats without boxes.
They got used to their new surroundings
and the people around them more quickly.
Something as simple as a cardboard box made a real difference.
So a box isn't just a toy for a cat.
It's more like a safe room.
When the world gets too loud the cat can duck inside
and shut it all out.
In there nothing can come at it from behind or from the side.
It only has to keep an eye on one small opening.
For a nervous animal that's a huge weight off its shoulders.
That's also why cats love all sorts of other small spaces.
Think about all the odd places you've found your cat over the years.
Your cat has probably curled up inside an open drawer.
It has probably squeezed under the bed or into the bathroom sink.
Laundry baskets and paper shopping bags are big favorites too.
Some cats wedge themselves onto a shelf between two rows of books.
All of those spots share one thing in common.
They wrap around the cat and make it feel snug and protected.
And remember how much time a cat spends asleep.
Most cats doze for a big part of every single day.
An animal that sleeps that much is going
to be very fussy about where it sleeps.
A sleeping cat can't keep watch. So it wants a spot
where nothing can sneak up on it while it naps.
A box gives it exactly that.

When a mother cat is about
to give birth she goes looking for a nest.
She wants somewhere dark and quiet and tucked well out of the way.
A closet floor or the back of a cupboard
or yes an old cardboard box.
If she feels the nest isn't safe enough
she may even carry her kittens somewhere new. She picks them up one

So the very first home most kittens

It's warm and it's dark and it's full of their mother's smell.

And this explains the fancy bed problem too.

The third reason is warmth.
Cats like to be a good deal warmer than we do.
Scientists talk about something called the thermoneutral zone.
That's the range of temperatures where an animal doesn't have
to burn any energy to warm up or cool down.
For people that zone sits somewhere around room temperature.
For cats it sits a lot higher.
It's roughly thirty to thirty six degrees Celsius.
That works out to about eighty six to ninety seven degrees Fahrenheit.
Most of our homes are quite a bit cooler than that.

It's why they sleep on top of warm laptops

And it's one more reason they love boxes.
Cardboard turns out to be a surprisingly good insulator.
It traps the warmth of the cat's body inside the box.
A small box holds that heat even better

So when your cat squeezes into a box

It has found itself a cozy little heater.
The fourth reason is that boxes are new and interesting.
An indoor cat lives in a pretty small world.
